entries.title: Mike Lee’s Threats to Nix August Recess Are Infuriate His Colleagues
entries.summary: How would canceling recess go over with Senate Republicans? “A total nonstarter,” one senior GOP aide said.
entries.content:
Senate Republican leaders are used to headaches from Utah Sen. Mike Lee, but the battle is reaching an apex as Lee attempts to derail the August recess and force another vote on President Donald Trump’s priority voting bill.

Lee said that he planned to object to the upper chamber’s planned five-week August recess “until such a time as the Senate has passed the SAVE America Act.” On Monday, Trump joined Lee’s call and demanded that the Senate cancel recess to push through the bill. Those loud, and very online, efforts are part of a deepening rift between Trump and members of Senate leadership, who have little interest in keeping the conference in town to take a perilous vote only months before the midterm elections.

Top Senate Republicans not only believe those votes would be a waste of time, but they would be politically problematic. Staying in session would preclude incumbent senators from campaigning back home, though senators who vote to give themselves a long summer break might have a difficult time explaining themselves to constituents.

"If I thought there was a path to getting a result, I'm all for it,” said Senate Majority Leader John Thune. “But if we are going to be sitting here and in endless quorum calls, I don't know if that's in anybody's best interest.”

Thune also noted that versions of the SAVE America Act have failed on five occasions to win simple majority support. Not only does it not have the requisite Democratic support to overcome a filibuster, there are not enough votes to weaken the 60-vote threshold in favor of a “talking” filibuster that Lee and Trump have repeatedly hailed.

“It’s an act of futility,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said of Trump’s call to cancel recess.

When asked how canceling recess to work on the voting bill would go over with members, one senior Senate GOP aide was blunt.

“A total nonstarter,” the aide said, adding that the “math doesn’t math.”

The Senate’s much-cherished August break is set to run from Aug. 7 until Sept. 13. House lawmakers fled Washington last week and are set to return the week before Labor Day.

As for Thune allies, much of the frustration since the start of the year has centered on Lee, who has led the messaging effort almost entirely through his rapid-fire X account.

A Lee-forced tally would force Republicans to take a difficult vote and, effectively, open them up to an uptick in criticism from conservative activists with massive followings and, potentially, the president.

“Of course,” Cornyn said when asked if Lee is putting members in a bad spot. “He’s demoralizing our base of voters we’re depending on in 99 days to elect Republicans. What possible rationale could there be for that other than self-aggrandizement.”

A pair of sources noted that outside of his social media postings, Lee has done little to try to sway skeptical colleagues — and is largely quiet during weekly Senate GOP lunches.

“The worst threat to a GOP majority: Mike Lee’s continued SAVE Act antics,” a second senior Senate GOP aide told NOTUS.

The second aide also noted that colleagues have frequently observed him scrolling through X on his phone and view his SAVE Act actions “as a ploy to become a social media star” rather than a serious legislative effort.

"I think it's snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. I think what we need to do is get out of here,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina). “Staying here longer and just assuming that because we're here, we're going to bridge some profound differences between people, is a catastrophic political miscalculation and shows that we're tone deaf to the fact that we have a real threat ahead of us with respect to losing the majority.”

“I want the Senate members home doing that, not doing the performative politics up here that people like Mike Lee want to do,” Tillis added.

Lee is not without allies: Sens. Rick Scott (R-Florida) and Ashley Moody (R-Florida) have joined his cause.

“While the Spartans said ‘come back with your shield, or on it,’ my demand is a lot easier: only return home if we carry the SAVE America Act as a prize for the whole country,” Lee said, defending his position, in a statement to NOTUS.

The timing of Lee’s pressure campaign could not be worse in the eyes of some in the conference, as Election Day is coming increasingly in view for members.

Democrats need to pick off four seats in November in order to take back the majority, and the road for them requires toppling a number of incumbent Republicans — with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) at the top of the list.

“People want to campaign,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), a member of Republican leadership. “I just came from inspecting floods and damage in my state. Staying connected is really important.”

Threats and calls to cancel the August break have become something of a tradition over the years.

Then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell canceled the first week of the break in 2017 for Republicans to work on health care after the late Sen. John McCain blocked the party’s “skinny repeal” effort.

Only a year later, the Kentucky Republican canceled more than two weeks of the break. The move kept a number of Senate Democrats at the Capitol and away from campaigning in their home states.

Republicans are expected to discuss how to handle recess in the coming days, including during conference-wide luncheons.

“It’ll be a week,” Capito said.
entries.author: Al Weaver

entries.title: Commanders’ David Blough Has Been Preparing for This Moment His Whole Life
entries.summary: Friends and former teammates say Washington’s new, 30-year-old coordinator is just the man to lead an offense.
entries.content:
Facing nearly insurmountable odds, David Blough was not fazed.

It was 2013, his senior season at Creekview High School in Carrollton, Texas, and the Mustangs were playing for a spot in the Class 4A playoffs.

Entering the fourth quarter, Creekview trailed North Forney, 26-13. Where some other teenage quarterbacks might succumb to defeat, Blough remained stoic. He walked the sideline, assuring his teammates everything was fine and they still had a whole quarter to play.

“He’s just walking around telling everybody,” said Creekview offensive coordinator Robert Paschall, a longtime high school coach in Texas. “It wasn't fake bullshit. I've seen fake bullshit, like people running around being hype. … This was ‘By God, we're gonna win.’”

At some point, Blough and Paschall noticed North Forney had difficulty covering flood routes, where multiple receivers go to one side of the field. They started spamming the playcall the rest of the way, and within a few possessions, they had erased the deficit — clinching a 33-29 win and earning Creekview’s first playoff berth in five years.

The moxie Blough displayed that night was an early indicator of the player and coach he would become — one who knows how to remain calm, lean on what works and take the lead. He showed it then as a three-star quarterback prospect with just one college offer, from Purdue. He showed it with the Boilermakers, once throwing for over 300 yards and three touchdowns in a rout of No. 2 Ohio State. And he showed it as an NFL backup, working his way from undrafted free agent to a five-year career in which he made seven starts.

Now, he’ll need those traits as the Commanders’ offensive coordinator, a role he inherits after just two years as an assistant coach. Starting this week at training camp, he will be tasked with cooking up a new offense that takes full advantage of Jayden Daniels, Washington's young franchise quarterback, and helps the team bounce back from a disastrous 2025 season.

The hardest part of this task? Blough is just 30 years old. And he’s never called plays before.

“He was always somebody we knew would develop into this role as a play caller,” Commanders coach Dan Quinn said of his young coordinator. “He came in as a coach ahead of the curve, so he had a bigger vision and perspective [than] maybe a coach just coming out of school or something in that space wouldn't.”

Save for his father, the most important and impactful men in Blough’s life have been his coaches. Because of them, he’s always had a strong passion for mentoring young people and giving back to his community. Those who’ve known Blough the longest say he was born to do this job.

“I've always wanted to build men,” Blough said. “And I've learned this is the closest thing I could ever do to calling a play in a huddle again is building it, creating it.”

David Blough Purdue 1 AP - 18288600829843 (3000x2003, AR: 1.50)

Leading from the front

Ask anyone from Blough’s childhood and they’ll tell you he has always been a leader.

In elementary school, Blough got the lead in the school musical despite not knowing how to really sing. A few years later his mother, LuAnn, signed him up for soccer even though Blough had never played before. "He went out and scored four goals," she said. When Blough was in middle school, he walked up to the coach of the football team and told him, "Hi, Coach, I'm your quarterback."

Andres Ruiz was Blough’s 7-on-7 coach in those early years. The ex-Marine said he used to push his young athletes hard, implementing some military tactics. No matter how tired Blough seemed, he never stopped trying to lift up his teammates.

“Even though he may not have been the most talented kid on the field, he was always front of the line, encouraging guys, keeping their heads up when they get tired, leading from the front,” Ruiz said.

Blough was always the one looking for extra reps, both on the field and in the weight room. By the time he got to high school, Blough — who started on varsity as a sophomore — would wake up teammates at the crack of dawn and wrangle them into throwing sessions.

“He would send me [a text message], ‘Well, our competition isn't sleeping in.’ And then it's like, ‘OK, you just rage-baited me into going to work out, and of course I want to work out,'” said Raul Bustillos, Creekview’s starting running back.

Blough’s known since high school that he wanted to be a coach. It might sound like an odd dream, but this was in Texas, home of Friday Night Lights. He once dressed up as legendary Cowboys coach Tom Landry, complete with the trademark fedora and blazer.

“It was like 95 degrees, so I don't think he wore it that long,” said Dylan Kittrell, the team’s receiver.

On the bus to games, Paschall would hand his teenage quarterback the playsheet and tell him to pick what he wanted to run. When Blough was asked why he picked a particular play, he’d explain his rationale in detail, saying he knew the safety would react a certain way or his receiver could get to a certain spot.

“He was very precise and exacting,” Paschall said.

David Blough Purdue 2 - AP - 672929643459 (832x553, AR: 1.50)

‘A designer, not a dictator’

John Shoop, Purdue’s offensive coordinator, came to Carrollton for a recruiting visit during Blough’s junior season. But there was a mix-up with the school, and no showcase on the schedule. Instead, Blough organized his own throwing session on the fly with about 10 of his teammates.

That day, Shoop said he witnessed someone who showed command of an offense and clearly garnered so much respect from his teammates that they’d drop everything to shine a brighter light on him. Shoop, who was an assistant coach with the Carolina Panthers from 1995 to 1998, said he hadn’t seen anything like that since evaluating future MVP quarterback Steve McNair out of Alcorn State in the mid 1990s.

“It was really revealing to me,” Shoop said of Blough’s showcase.

Blough committed to Purdue in 2013. After his second season, the school hired former Louisville quarterback Jeff Brohm as its new head coach. Early on, Brohm asked his players to bring him ideas for plays if they ever had any, assuming no one would actually take him up on the offer. Blough did. The coach allowed his quarterback to script his own plays at times, and away from the field Blough designed his own playbook in his free time.

“He was not shy about that, which was outstanding, because a lot of people don't fully get invested that much,” said Brohm, who had planned to hire his former quarterback as a graduate assistant in 2018 before Blough signed as an undrafted free agent with Lions. “And I think when he did that you knew at some point down the road, ‘OK, this guy's gonna be a good coach, because he really, really is into this.’”

In addition to passion, Blough always had composure. While his former coaches admit to losing their cool sometimes, they say Blough has never been the type. He is never frantic. He has an empathy that doesn’t allow mistakes or a lack of discipline to turn into anger. When he does raise his voice, it's more encouraging than demeaning.

“Some quarterbacks are kind of a-holes,” said Kittrell. “And others are able to teach it to everyone.”

“I truly believe that I am a designer, not a dictator,” Blough said, referring to a philosophy he learned from author Martin E. P. Seligman’s book “Flourish: A Visionary New Understanding of Happiness and Well-being.”

When Blough found out that his college teammate, running back Markell Jones, was in Purdue’s aviation school, the competitor in him came out: If Markell can do it, I can do it too. So he began studying to earn his private pilot license, work you can still find on his LinkedIn page. Jones, now a pilot for United Airlines, said the studies speak to Blough’s competitive nature, which can be infectious to those around him.

“When David was speaking to our team, everyone locked in,” Jones said. “You could look on his face and see that David's going to go down dying. David will die to get the job done to execute the play to the best of his ability.”

David Blough Stafford - AP - 19272641514742 (2771x1847, AR: 1.50)

No surprise

No matter how much of a whiz kid Blough may be or how good a high school and college quarterback he was, he has never been an offensive coordinator. Teams hiring first-time play callers have had uneven results over the years: In the NFC East alone, the Cowboys’ Kellen Moore led a top-10 offense in his first season as a play caller in 2019 while the Eagles’ Brian Johnson and Kevin Patullo were each fired following single seasons in 2023 and 2025, respectively.

But that’s the paradox of experience: You can only gain it from doing the job, but oftentimes you can’t get the job without it.

Blough, who will be making a rare and sizable leap from assistant quarterbacks coach to coordinator, said that imposter syndrome is almost unavoidable.

“I think everybody at some point who's made it to this level, whether it's our quarterback or head coach or head chef down there probably feels imposter syndrome in some way,” Blough said. “And then you prepare really hard and you believe in what you're doing, and there's a trust established between who you're doing it with, and it helps ease all that.”

One of Blough’s best traits, former teammates and coaches say, is understanding both the tendencies of the defense and the characteristics of his own roster. It’s something he picked up from Paschall, whose offensive system at Creekview was simple: maximize what each individual player was good at and avoid what they were bad at.

Rumors have swirled for months about the Commanders signing another starting receiver to pair with veteran Terry McLaurin, but for someone with Blough’s mentality, it’s less about who you can add and more about making the most of the players available.

“We put Terry and Antonio [Williams] and Treylon [Burks] and Dyami [Brown] … in the best position possible to go be successful, and that gives me confidence, knowing that they're the best in the world at what they do. I just get to help facilitate that,” Blough said.

But his transition to coordinator, like all major transitions, will not be without hiccups. Throughout last month’s team activities, there were mishaps on offense: fumbled snaps, overthrows, interceptions, false starts and bobbled handoffs. But that’s just part of the process, according to Blough. It’s better to make those mistakes now, he says, and learn from them rather than commit a false start in the playoffs when the game is on the line.

“We know that if we're worth our salt as coaches and able to correct and teach, that you know when it's fourth and 4 in the biggest stage, we'll be able to make the play, because we've communicated and committed to excellence,” Blough said.

Blough is still cagey about what the offense will actually look like this season, other than acknowledging that Daniels will take more snaps under center, McLaurin will line up all over the formation, and he plans to change up tempo and personnel groupings more to make the offense unpredictable.

But in the small glimpses of his play-calling, Blough has shown the ability to take advantage of a defense.

During a 2024 matchup with the Eagles, Blough, still the team’s assistant quarterbacks coach, was behind what became the game-winning play: a 9-yard touchdown pass from Daniels to receiver Jamison Crowder. Blough had helped design the red-zone play — empty backfield, trips left, mirrored post routes toward the back of the end zone — years earlier for a different team. The Commanders practiced it earlier that week during two-minute drills. In the moment, with the game on the line, Blough delivered.

Quinn is betting big that Blough will help Washington return to the playoffs following last season’s catastrophic 5-12 finish. But for every bit of confidence the head coach has in his new coordinator, those that have been on this journey with Blough the longest are twice as certain he will succeed.

“In that league, people don't care if you're 20, people don't care if you're 60,” said Shoop, who has known Blough since college. “If you can help them get good, they listen to you, and Dave can help people get good. He really can. He's clearly done it.”

“All of this, to someone looking at it from the outside in, it probably looks like a surprise,” said Kittrell, who has known Blough even longer. “But for us, people that know him and are close with him, it's not a surprise whatsoever.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Lawmakers Are Riding the AI Wave to Stardom
entries.summary: Politicians who can speak to the high-profile issue are positioned to grow their credibility among voters and with their party.
entries.content:
Artificial intelligence is upending the internet, warfare, science and the economy. It is also disrupting power in Washington by providing a pathway to relevance for politicians willing to grapple with it.

Ask lawmakers on Capitol Hill who work on AI policy why they’re doing it, and they’ll tell you it’s one of the most pressing issues of our time. Observers point out it’s also politically astute of them to embrace the issue: It’s a fast track to higher name recognition, credibility within their party and the groundwork for a platform to run on.

“Whenever there's a developing policy or technology that’s also in the news a lot, you always have a lot of ambitious politicians who love to go running towards the light,” said Eddie Vale, a Democratic political consultant.

“It is definitely growing exponentially, both in terms of like groups and also politicians trying to get involved,” Vale told NOTUS. “When AI first came out, people were thinking about it more as a tech policy issue, but as people learned more about it, they realized it is starting to impact almost every policy area.”

In practice, that means members of Congress across the political spectrum have introduced hundreds of bills aimed at shaping how AI is developed and used. While few AI-related bills have passed, AI regulation is becoming a prized policy space which can be leveraged for political power.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, argued AI policy is going to be “a decisive issue” in the 2028 presidential election and beyond. Casar isn’t considered a possible 2028 candidate, but he has recently introduced bills to protect children using AI chatbots and stop AI-powered algorithmic pricing. He’s also proposed taxing large companies' AI use.

“Democrats have this huge opportunity to be on the side of everyday people and leave JD Vance and the Republicans on the side of scumbags like David Sacks and Elon Musk,” Casar told NOTUS.

But it’s not just Democrats whose careers could end up being hoisted by AI.

Three-term Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California) has long been the point person in the House Republican Conference for AI policy. He co-led a bipartisan AI working group that established the largest bipartisan AI regulatory framework in Congress. Earlier this year, he became the conference policy chair.

When NOTUS asked Obernolte, who was previously a computer scientist and game developer in California, if AI has boosted his career in Congress, he said he hadn't “really thought about it.”
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)“For most of us, this is not why we’re doing this. We’re doing this because we care deeply about this issue and we feel that federal action is desperately necessary,” Obernolte said. “We rely on silos of expertise ... on the issues having to do with technology policy, those of us that have a background in technology, I think, we have people that listen to us.”

That background may have helped land his spot in leadership, according to Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), who was policy chair before Obernolte and endorsed him for the role.

“He's done a lot of work on many things, but he’s somebody who certainly understands AI,” Hern told NOTUS. “And that's an area where we have quite a deficiency in Congress. Maybe even more so on the House side.”

“He’s somebody who is obviously educated on it. And I've always said I want people talking about important issues that have actually had experience on the outside, and he's certainly the right person,” Hern added.

Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), who is planning to run for vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus in the next Congress, according to a source familiar with her thinking, recently joined forces with Obernolte to introduce an AI safety bill. The bill would allow the federal government to intervene in the deployment of AI models and create safety transparency requirements for AI companies. Her involvement drew criticism from some members of her party after the release of a discussion draft last month which included language that could limit state-level AI regulation, a policy that is toxic among many Democrats.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)The lawmakers have reportedly continued to make changes to their proposal, but early on it managed to get support from some AI safety advocates and AI industry insiders, which could translate into credibility for her leadership bid.

“Taking on big problems and working across the aisle to solve them is what folks back home elected me to do,” Trahan told NOTUS in a statement. “Automation and offshoring took our jobs a generation ago ... Is this good politics? That's not really how I think about this work. But sure, good politics is being responsive to the people you represent.”

“There's earth-shattering AI news practically every week. It's only going to get more frequent and more serious as these models get more powerful,” she added. “Every member of Congress knows next week will bring something else just as alarming, if not worse. We're responding with the urgency this moment demands.”

The specifics of how AI will change the future remain uncertain, but for people jumping on AI regulation, the uncertainty in the space is part of the appeal.

“It's just the next frontier of policymaking, you know? You can't be here knowing that we're in an era of technological advances and, you know, still on a rotary phone,” Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-New York) told NOTUS.

Candidates are also seeing the political opportunity around focusing on AI and staking their campaigns on it, with mixed results.

In June, New York State Assembly member Alex Bores lost his bid in a Democratic primary to replace retiring Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-New York) after making AI regulation a central part of his campaign; AI-backed super PACs spent millions of dollars in the race both for and against him. Abdul El-Sayed, who’s running to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), released a populist AI policy agenda that includes public ownership of AI companies. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tennessee), who is running for governor in her state, has leaned heavily into AI regulation with a platform that would create protections for children using AI chatbots and safety standards for AI companies.
Election 2026 Michigan (5029x3353, AR: 1.50)“AI, being arguably the most important technology of our time, both in the immediate future and long-term future, will continue to attract a lot of people. Many are trying to get in early at the ground floor,” Caleb Knapp, an AI safety lobbyist at the Alliance for Secure AI, told NOTUS.

“A lot of folks both anticipate and are expecting AI to become much more of a kitchen-table issue because of how it impacts culture and the economy and everything in between,” he said.

Other candidates who might be angling for a presidential to run in 2028 have also tried to shape the AI regulation debate.

Vice President JD Vance, who has long advocated for a relaxed AI regulatory state, has recently advocated for stronger restrictions on the technology. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) has made AI populism central to his politics, advocating for strict regulations that would bar kids from using AI chatbots and force safety-compliance measures for AI companies. And Gavin Newsom, the Democratic governor of California who signed one of the first AI safety laws in the country, has said the U.S. government should own a stake in large AI companies.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)Some members of Congress whose districts house tech companies, and therefore whose work on AI regulation began years ago, argue that the public is pressuring more candidates to weigh in on the issue.

“People are getting more and more questions by their constituents back home, so it's understandable that they're waking up to the issue,” Rep. Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat who represents parts of Silicon Valley, told NOTUS.

And others say they welcome the input of more members of Congress.

“It's a good thing that more of my colleagues are rolling up their sleeves on this issue,” Rep. Sam Liccardo, another Silicon Valley Democrat, told NOTUS. “Ambition in this regard can be positive because for too long, too few of us have been delving into the details.”

entries.title: What $1.2 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
entries.content:
What does $1.2 million get you in the D.C. area? We found listings in the District, Maryland and Virginia that fit the bill.

(Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.)

D.C.

Untitled
The Listing: 2501 M St. NW, Unit T04

The Price: $1,200,000

The Specifics: This two-bedroom, three-bathroom condo, which was built in 2017, comes in at just under 1,500 square feet and features what listing agent Matt Cheney describes as a “masterclass in modern design.” Interior highlights include white oak floors and lots of natural light. The building features a number of amenities, including a fitness center, a club room with a bar and a front desk that’s staffed 24 hours a day.

The Neighborhood: The building is located in West End near the border of Georgetown and is close to Foggy Bottom. There are several restaurants and stores within walking distance, including Nobu, Trader Joe’s and Whole Foods.

Maryland

Untitled
The Listing: 1118 Orchard Way, Silver Spring, Md.

The Price: $1,200,000

The Specifics: This four-bedroom, five-bathroom home totaling more than 4,800 square feet is located at the end of a quiet road and borders a large, wooded park. The interior style is midcentury modern, with highlights including the fireplace and cathedral ceilings in the living room. The one-acre lot includes a long driveway, two large garages, a fenced vegetable garden and a well-maintained lawn that features peach and plum trees.

The Neighborhood: The home is located in the Colesville Farm Estates neighborhood of Silver Spring, which consists of large single-family homes on spacious, private lots. Downtown D.C. is roughly a 40-minute drive.

Virginia

Untitled
The Listing: 1302 Quincy St., Alexandria, Va.

The Price: $1,150,000

The Specifics: This 4-bedroom, 2-bathroom home totaling 2,000 square feet was originally built as a stone cottage in 1949 by two Italian brothers and has been remodeled and expanded over the years, including several recent upgrades. Highlights include a wood-burning fireplace in the living and dining area, an expansive primary suite with a reading nook on the second floor and a fenced-in yard with a back patio.

The Neighborhood: North Ridge is an historic, affluent neighborhood in Alexandria, located 5 miles south of downtown Washington, D.C. (roughly a 25-minute drive). Old Town Alexandria is 15 minutes away.

entries.title: Democrats May Break FISA Blockade if Jay Clayton Gets Confirmed
entries.summary: While Democrats may not support Clayton, they say he’s better to head the intelligence community than Bill Pulte.
entries.content:
The Senate is one step closer to reauthorizing a crucial spy powers tool that lapsed in June after voting to move past a procedural hurdle Monday on the way to confirming Jay Clayton as the director of national intelligence.

Democrats have blocked the reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act for more than a month over their concerns with the acting head of national intelligence, Bill Pulte, who has been criticized for his lack of experience and his immediate slashing of jobs in the umbrella agency for the U.S. intelligence community.

With Clayton’s confirmation vote scheduled for Tuesday, Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said his side of the aisle is more open to renewing the program if Pulte is out and Clayton is in –– although it’s still not a done deal.

“We've got to get a new DNI in,” Warner said. “I'm not supporting Mr. Clayton, but it'll be a vast improvement.”

Reauthorizing FISA will require 60 votes to get past the Senate filibuster, and with some Republican opposition, Democrats would need to round out the numbers.

Warner did not say which further concessions Democrats might want to see in order to renew the surveillance program, but said the fact that telecommunication providers are still operating under the expired law gives the caucus more leeway in negotiations.

“We're not under the time crunch that we anticipated because the communication providers are still cooperating,” Warner said. “This was always going to be a lift. The majority of my caucus probably won't support it … but those of us who are in this national security environment understand it's got to get done.”

The Senate Intelligence Committee advanced Clayton’s nomination last week in a party-line vote, even though he declined to answer questions about the legitimacy of the 2020 election. Warner, however, has acknowledged Clayton’s experience with intelligence matters; Clayton is currently the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.

Senate Republicans had initially hoped that Clayton’s nomination would push Democrats to extend FISA before it expired in June, a plan that was derailed after Trump instructed Clayton not to attend his hearing.

Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, the Senate Republican whip, told reporters last week that he hopes Clayton’s nomination will continue to move FISA forward.

“The idea is to get things moving along as quickly as we can,” Barrasso said. “I want to get FISA reauthorized. I want to get the confirmation done. One has to be done before the other, and we expect to have him confirmed shortly.”

Some Democrats on the intelligence panel told NOTUS that Clayton’s appointment is enough for them to back FISA reauthorization.

“When Bill Pulte is no longer the acting DNI, I think there's a path forward for FISA,” said Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona). “The hurdle is for the current, acting DNI to get that out of the way, and I think there's a path to try to expedite this.”

Sen. Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, echoed Kelly, emphasizing that although Clayton is not the perfect candidate, it is time to renew the surveillance tool.

“I’m ready to,” King said when asked if he’d support reauthorization. “We’ve got a DNI in place, and then I’m ready to move forward.”

But other Democrats said they’ll continue to oppose renewing the surveillance program altogether, even under a new intelligence director. Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey), a former State Department adviser, told NOTUS he’s long had problems with FISA –– especially under the Trump administration.

“They made matters worse by bringing in Pulte, and that shook my confidence about what they're going to do with Clayton or anybody,” Kim said. “It doesn’t redress the underlying problems we had about the role of privacy and the role of the courts.”

Even with enough Democratic support, the Senate may not hold a vote to renew the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act until members return in September. The House doesn’t return until the end of August, and the Senate has stacked up a pile of must-pass items before lawmakers depart for their own summer recess.
entries.author: Avani Kalra

entries.title: Max Scherzer Is Still in the Fight. These Nats Are, Too.
entries.summary: Five years after his trade kicked off the Nationals' rebuild, the World Series hero returned to his former home.
entries.content:
A man spent his 42nd birthday pitching at Nationals Park on Monday night. And then everyone clapped for him. And then Max Scherzer waved.

And then … OK, wait. Look. There’s a lot going on with the Nationals this week, important baseball things that, practically speaking, matter way more than looking back. When the present’s good, when life suddenly goes from bleh to exciting again, you don’t have to grip so tight to the past any longer, which is maybe just a winding description of happiness. And after losing, 3-2, to open a series against the struggling Blue Jays, the Nats keep hanging at 54-53, explosive on offense but still too imbalanced to pull much further from .500. With six days until the trade deadline, they’re right on the edge of the wild-card race, meaning the reasons to buy or sell — or to do some combination of the two — feel like one of those DIY detective boards, the colored strings connecting a bunch of little clues.

Depending, of course, on the player and the offers, could a couple of wins or losses really make a difference? Could, in theory, a single series determine whether the team trades Foster Griffin? Luis García Jr.? What about, gulp, CJ Abrams?

That’s how Blake Butera, the team’s first-year manager, is talking. That’s how Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, has talked in recent interviews, too. The Nats are still exploring all options, which wouldn’t be news around here if not for the last five Julys, when there was no strategic gray area, just different forms of dread.

“The last thing we want to do here is play games where it doesn’t really matter, right?” Butera said before Monday’s game. “We want to avoid that as long as possible. I know I haven’t been at this level, but in the minor leagues I never coached a game in August or September that was like: ‘Oh we’re out of it and we’re just trying to get to the end of the season and we have to get into the offseason.’ I don’t want to know what that feels like. What’s going on right now …”

And that’s when Butera started tapping the table in front of him.

Quick taps, like he was testing a microphone.

“How these games feel and how important each one seems to be, is what I want to feel and I think what we all want to feel for as long as possible.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Which sounds a lot like when Max Scherzer was on the team. Which is why, no matter how much is happening right now, trade deadline or otherwise, Monday might have made you feel something else, something raw, something about how it once was and how fast it all goes. Was it the way he kept throwing his arms out, just like he used to, as if they’ll fall off if he stops moving them? The solo walk — no, stalk — from the bullpen before the top of the first? Those waves before he exited to a standing ovation, quite possibly for the last time in this stadium, right as he stepped on the P in an on-field advertisement for AARP?

I bet it was the waves.

“The great moments that we had with my time here in D.C., those are just things you never forget,” Scherzer said after the game. “So coming back here is a good trip down memory lane.”

Scherzer, more than any active player, is a reminder of very good days in Washington, of moments and seasons that will stretch into forever. There used to be his blue and brown eyes above right field and now it’s a Toyota ad. But if you, like me, are into connecting narrative dots, he’s also a reminder of how long it’s been since this city could feel what it’s feeling this month. That each game can mean something. That it’s not pointless to care.

Five years ago this week, the dread began. That was when, after a team with Scherzer, Trea Turner, Juan Soto and a hobbled Kyle Schwarber wasn’t good enough, the Nats completed a full teardown by trading Scherzer and Turner to the Dodgers. For Nationals fans, the half decade since had brought little joy until this season. And for Scherzer, it’s included stops in L.A., New York, Texas and Toronto, which has all aged him a good bit, which is what happens in baseball when you’re 42 and not ready to quit the only adult job you’ve ever had.

Forearm and back issues have limited him to 24 ⅔ innings this year. On Monday, in his first start back from the injured list, he needed 75 pitches to record eight outs, which meant his night ended before the third inning did. He labored right away, loading the bases in the first before stranding the three runners. In the second, García, the only current Nat who played with Scherzer, tagged him for an RBI double. Then to finish his outing, Scherzer struck out Daylen Lile, who was 4 when the Diamondbacks drafted Scherzer in the first round in 2006.

“We’re all getting old,” Scherzer said of himself and Justin Verlander (and also everyone, in theory). “All of our bodies are not quite the same.”But the stadium wasn’t dotted with Scherzer jerseys because anyone expected him to dominate. No, it was dotted with his name, with his No. 31 in white and red, because of what he meant to you, you and yes, you, too, because your heart wasn’t always so cold. Because for six and a half years, Scherzer did what so few athletes can, which was make almost everything he did must-watch, all the way down to how he vibrated in the dugout. Because he once pitched a day after breaking his nose, when his right eye — the blue one — looked as if it had been jabbed by Mike Tyson. Because when he did dominate, it looked like two Cy Young Awards, two no-hitters and a World Series ring.

Twice in his postgame interview Monday, he threw out buzz phrases from the 2019 title run, which are apparently burned into his vocabulary. He said the Blue Jays just have to go 1-0 every day. He said, when asked about striking out Lyle, that it’s just a matter of staying in the fight, especially with how hard it’s been for him to stick on the mound.

Five years is long enough to change a lot of things. But it’s also, in this small corner of the universe, long enough for things to start changing back.

entries.title: Pipe Dream
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: sky-high utility bills, development delays and the Commanders’ new offensive coordinator.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

THE LATEST

Gas is now fueling the ongoing debate over high utility bills in D.C.

The D.C. Public Service Commission is holding a pair of hearings this week on Washington Gas’ ongoing plans to replace its aging pipes across the city. Over the last decade, some 50 miles of pipes — some dating back to the 1940s — have been swapped out; the utility company told NOTUS that continuing the effort is “essential to maintaining a safe, reliable, and resilient energy system for the more than 160,000 customers we serve in the District.”

But opponents worry about the impact on residential bills and the environment. The next three-year pipe replacement plan is expected to cost $150 million, and D.C. consumers will see those costs factored into their monthly bills. That would come on top of rising Pepco bills, which the Public Service Commission is similarly getting heat for.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb is opposed to Washington Gas’ plan. He says the pipe replacements thus far have been too expensive and have failed to contain some leaks. Environmental groups like the Sierra Club would rather see D.C. fully phase out natural gas and turn toward building electrification and renewable energy.

Some experts say replacing aging pipes in D.C. is critical. Speaking to the D.C. Council last month, former federal regulator Cynthia Quarterman said the city has more 1940s-vintage cast-iron gas pipes than almost anywhere else. “A jurisdiction with the nation’s highest concentration of the nation’s most dangerous pipe material is the last jurisdiction that should slow down,” she said.

The Public Service Commission will use the two hearings to craft the specifics of the next portion of Washington Gas’ pipe replacement plans. The utility says it is focused on “completing this work efficiently and responsibly, while keeping customer affordability top of mind.” But Schwalb wants any approved plan to “keep the community safe from dangerous gas leaks … and protect ratepayers from excessive and unwarranted rate increases.”

Utility prices will be back on the commission’s docket in October, when regulators will again take up a controversial multiyear rate increase requested by Pepco.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Start your engines. Construction is underway at the National Mall, where the Freedom 250 Grand Prix will take place next month, ABC7 reports.

There are delays on Metro’s Red Line — just not the ones you’re used to. A plan for a 434-unit residential development on the Takoma Metro station’s parking lot is facing setbacks due to high construction costs, challenges securing financing and complications delivering promised affordable units, reports UrbanTurf. Delays are nothing new for the project, which has been floating around for at least 15 years and hit just about every bureaucratic, political and civic snag possible.





FROM VIRGINIA

The son of Eric Bieniemy, the Commanders’ former offensive coordinator, has been arrested and charged with shooting his mother in their Ashburn home, The Associated Press reports.





FROM MARYLAND

A Montgomery County Council member said last week that firefighters violated a county law prohibiting voluntary ICE cooperation, The Banner reports.




GUESS THE LISTING

d323f1a1d8a2a93d630107276eac9e99-uncropped_scaled_within_1536_1152 copy.jpg (1350x900, AR: 1.50)Listed for $1,200,000, this four-bedroom, five-bathroom home totaling more than 4,800 square feet features cathedral ceilings and two large garages.

Guess where this listing is sold:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.
We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.





SPORTS

The Commanders’ new offensive coordinator is young — very young. At 30 years old, David Blough is not far removed from his NFL playing days. Now, as training camp gets underway this week, the former quarterback is tasked with bringing Washington’s offense back to life.

In a deep-dive profile, NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson talked to Blough’s friends, family and former teammates about what makes him the man for the job.

In soccer news, the Spirit are now two points clear at the top of the NWSL table after a win against Denver Summit FC over the weekend.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Blue Jays, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Sun, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Andrew Burton. Photo courtesy of HomeVisit Photography. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) wine. A special shout-out to David Shaw, who answered first.

entries.title: Bibi’s Senate Fan Club
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Netanyahu’s Senate defenders. Democrats furrow their brows at the DNC. Republicans grumble about Mike Lee. Unblocking FISA. Two names to watch as AI policy grows. One last Michigan Senate primary debate. A conversation with Genevieve McDonald. And: Another campaign gets ripped off. 





THE LATEST

Senate Republicans are sticking with Benjamin Netanyahu even as public polling shows most Americans have little to no confidence in the Israeli prime minister to “do the right thing regarding world affairs.” Netanyahu will meet with many Republican senators, and Donald Trump, during his visit to Washington. Today, he’ll attend the memorial service for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Bibi’s strongest allies in the GOP.

It’s ironically a time of a relatively large split between Trump and Netanyahu, with the former theoretically trying to bring the Iran war to an end and the latter saying the only real end is regime change. Again, polling shows the American public never really bought into the war Bibi and Trump launched to begin with.

We tried to find out if there’s been a shift on Netanyahu’s leadership among Republicans as the war drags on. It was not readily apparent. “I think we should listen to Bibi Netanyahu on the issue of Iran,” Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) told us.

There’s no apparent YOLO Caucus on this issue. “I think we ought to help Israel all they need,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). “They’re a good, important ally.”

Senate Democrats are sticking with Ken Martin: This weekend’s string of embarrassingly bad coverage of the goings-on at the Democratic National Committee was greeted with furrowed brows of concern among the Senate caucus last night, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic reports. No Democrats we talked to called for Martin to step aside. It’s “up to the DNC to decide how they want to handle,” said Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada). Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) said Martin inherited a bad situation, but did draw one line.

“You should not throw things at staff,” he said, referring to reports that Martin threw a phone toward (but did not hit) an aide.

Open tabs: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow New Mail-In Voting Rules (NOTUS); McConnell says he is unable to return to US Senate yet (Reuters); Judge dismisses challenge to Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission (The Hill); Democratic Hill offices employ more interns (Legistorm)





From the Hill


“A total nonstarter” is how one senior Republican Senate aide responded to Trump’s suggestion that the chamber should cancel August recess to stay in D.C. and vote on the SAVE America Act (which they cannot pass, because there are not enough Republican senators willing to end the filibuster). NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports that the already grouchy conference is extra salty over the suggestion they stick around next month. Trump’s Senate SAVE Man, Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), has said he’ll object to the usual unanimous consent to start recess, potentially forcing Republicans to take a tough vote in favor of working from home Aug. 8 to Sept. 13.

“The worst threat to a GOP majority: Mike Lee’s continued SAVE Act antics,” a second senior Senate GOP aide told NOTUS.

Changes with Clayton: The Senate is scheduled to vote on whether to confirm Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence today. If confirmed, some Democrats say that could be enough for them to support the reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports.

“The hurdle is for the current, acting DNI to get that out of the way, and I think there’s a path to try to expedite this,” Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) said.

Riding the AI policy wave: Fluency in the thorny political questions around artificial intelligence is an increasingly valuable currency in Washington, NOTUS’ Samuel Larreal reports. Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California), the Republican conference policy chair, landed the leadership gig earlier this year in part due to his AI literacy, according to Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), who held the job before Obernolte and endorsed him to take over. And Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts) has raised her profile as a result of her work with Obernolte on AI safety. (A source says Trahan is planning to run for vice chair of the Democratic caucus next year.)

From the campaign trail


Haley Stevens’ fight night: The establishment pick for the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan came prepared for the final televised debate of the contest last night, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports from Southfield. Fresh off a wave of endorsements from respected Democratic officials in the state, Stevens took her chance to show voters she has more to offer than viral clips might indicate. She was feisty against the corporate- and AIPAC-stooge accusations coming at her from progressive opponent Abdul El-Sayed. “I am beholden to the people of Michigan,” she said.

It was by no means a lopsided loss for El-Sayed, Alex tells us. He continually attacked Stevens over the special interests funding her campaign and appeared to gain momentum as the debate went on. In keeping with the general theme of the race, Stevens won the half that aired on TV and El-Sayed did better in the half that aired only online.

Genevieve McDonald speaks out: The former political director of Graham Platner’s Senate campaign, who resigned last October and warned the campaign could end basically exactly like it did, is not buying the recent high-profile apology tour by top Platner strategist Morris Katz. “I don’t believe him,” McDonald told Alex. “I mean, consultants shouldn’t have main character energy. We have lost the plot when consultants are doing PR tours for themselves, for their own redemption, and that is what this felt like.”





NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

Local news: What $1.2 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia Real Estate, by Torrie Herrington

Sports desk: Commanders’ David Blough Has Been Preparing for This Moment His Whole Life, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

Rogers robbed: Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ joint fundraising committee lost about $16,700 after a vendor’s email was hacked and the committee unknowingly paid a deceptive invoice, NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno reports.

Campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet told Taylor that the campaign wasn’t able to get the money back.

Though the sum is paltry compared to the $1.5 million Rogers’ campaign has raised this election cycle, it’s the latest example of financial crimes targeting political campaigns — and the costs could go up if the criminals get bolder.





NOT US

  • ‘Climate hushing’ has swept the Democratic Party. New polling suggests it’s a mistake. By Kate Yoder for Grist
  • Congress Budgeted Billions for Big Transit Projects. Trump Isn’t Spending It. By Emily Badger and Alicia Parlapiano for The New York Times
  • A desert town may run out of water. Others could face the same fate. By Hannah Knowles for The Washington Post
  • How Bots Took Over Our Lives, by T.M. Brown for The New Yorker




Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr and Andrew Burton. Photo by Ronen Zvulun/Pool via AP.

entries.title: U.S. Delegation Storms Out of UN Meeting Over Criticism From France
entries.summary: The two longtime allies are embroiled in a feud over human rights policy.
entries.content:
The United States delegation to the United Nations walked out of a security council meeting this week during a speech by France that sharply criticized U.S. human rights stances, including comparing U.S. foreign policy to that of authoritarian nations.

A representative for the United States addressed the strained relations between the two longtime allies following the walkout, saying that it would continue to protest France’s actions as long as it sought to second-guess President Donald Trump’s foreign policy priorities.

“This disingenuous grandstanding is tiresome, but we have tolerated it out of a sense of comradery and mutual respect,” said U.S. Ambassador Dan Negrea, who serves as an alternate representative to the U.N.’s General Assembly, adding that the delegation would continue to walk out until France abandons its “condescending and disrespectful rhetoric.”

The meeting, which addressed Russia’s war against Ukraine, came mere days after the U.N.’s General Assembly opened a rift between the U.S. and allied nations over a vote to confirm Volker Türk for a second four-year term as the chief human rights officer for the organization.

Türk has been an outspoken critic of Israel’s war on Gaza and publicly criticized the U.S. government for its handling of its war with Iran. The U.S. previously accused Türk of leading the organization’s human rights mission “to its deathbed.”

Türk was confirmed by 144 member nations. Quickly after the vote, the U.S. denounced Volker’s confirmation as “another example of the UN’s inherent corruption and incompetence.” At least 10 countries voted against Volker’s nomination alongside the U.S., including Israel, North Korea, and Russia.

Before the walkout, the U.S. and France’s delegations shared heated exchanges online.

“The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore. Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it,” France’s mission to the UN posted on X.

“France voted for someone who has been lecturing, free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors,” U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz responded.

Under the Trump administration the U.S., which had historically been the U.N.’s largest financial contributor, has cut funding by more than $8 billion to U.N. specialized agencies and peacekeeping missions.

entries.title: The Secret Service Is Spending $90M to Supersize its Force
entries.summary: The agency is looking for 80,000 applicants. One contract to hit half of that goal is already breaking records.
entries.content:
The Secret Service awarded a $90 million contract to an untested firm this month for a nationwide advertising campaign aimed at recruiting thousands of personnel ahead of a grueling protective schedule in 2028.

The contract appears to be the largest the Secret Service has ever awarded to an outside company for recruitment, according to former officials and government records. And it sheds light on a hiring surge the Secret Service launched late last year to ease pressure on a workforce that has been understaffed for years.

The Secret Service wants the company to deliver more than 41,000 applicants in the next year, about half of the Secret Service’s overall goal of drawing about 80,000 applicants in that period, contracting documents say.

“That’s a massive campaign for them. It’s unprecedented,” said a former senior homeland security official familiar with Secret Service operations, who requested anonymity to discuss the contract.

Secret Service leaders have said they want to hire 4,000 new employees by 2028 to reduce burnout from an unforgiving operational tempo and make up for an attrition of experienced agents, which current and former officials say has worsened in recent months.

Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi said in a statement that the agency’s recruitment campaign is designed to “rightsize and properly staff the agency to meet the demands of a significantly heightened mission.”

“Through the federal procurement process, the agency selected a strategic marketing partner to support recruitment goals,” he said.

The Secret Service received $1.2 billion in a sweeping reconciliation package last year, including for recruiting, retention incentives and recruitment bonuses. Still, as of May, the agency had gained fewer than 400 employees since President Donald Trump took office, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management.

Secret Service leaders are racing to staff up for a 2028 security calendar that includes the presidential campaign, party conventions and the Olympic Games in Los Angeles. If the agency meets its hiring goals, it would expand by about 20%, topping 10,000 employees for the first time in its history.

The $90 million award went to a small contractor, Avvy LLC, based in Fairfax, Virginia, which has never previously won a federal contract.

Avvy is on the hook for producing advertisements on television, radio and streaming services, including during prime time. Streaming videos should generate 84 million impressions in the first year, while streaming audio ads should result in 140 million, contract documents state.

The contract calls for non-skippable video ads and streaming audio ads running in Washington, D.C., and 10 states, including Texas, Florida and Georgia. The ads are supposed to target people ages 20 to 39 who are involved in law enforcement, the military, or are veterans, according to contracting documents.

Guglielmi said the contractor will support Secret Service staff in recruiting and event logistics, but the Secret Service “remains responsible for evaluating applicants and making all hiring decisions.” He added that in-person events had accelerated the hiring process, but “no qualification, suitability, security or training standards have been reduced or eliminated.”

The scope of the contract highlights how the Secret Service is casting a wide net for its candidates, only a small fraction of whom make it through the agency’s arduous hiring process.

Some former homeland security officials cautioned that such a large batch of applicants could create bottlenecks in hiring, training and onboarding. Secret Service agents train for months alongside other federal law enforcement recruits at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, before spending several more months training in eastern Maryland and then joining field offices around the country.

That will require a delicate accommodation at FLETC, which is still moving through new hires to support Trump’s surge of immigration personnel. FLETC paused training for most non-Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel for several months last year as part of that push.

“None of the demands they’ve placed on FLETC for surge training have been realistic,” a current FLETC trainer, who requested anonymity over fear of reprisal, said of the administration’s efforts.

One former Secret Service official who handled personnel matters questioned whether the agency has enough workers to vet prospective agents and send them into the field in time to make a significant difference in the 2028 workload.

“The bottom-line question is still: The company delivers 41,000 applicants, then what?” said the former official, who requested anonymity to discuss the situation. “You still can’t get them on the street. Maybe you put them in a holding pattern and work from there.”

The former official added that while the Secret Service, like other law enforcement agencies, had struggled to hire, “That doesn’t mean $90 million just to get applicants is a smart idea.”

Many applicants don’t make it through the process to begin with. Background checks and a notoriously exacting polygraph exam screen many candidates out. Recently, questions about drug usage and financial issues have disqualified some young recruits, according to people familiar with the process. Officials say the physical fitness exam has also been a growing barrier for many candidates.

The Secret Service offers recruitment bonuses of $40,000 or more, but it faces competition from other law enforcement agencies offering similar incentives and roughly equal pay for less demanding work.

“They’ve got a lot of forces conspiring against them,” the former senior homeland security official said.

The Secret Service has seen some positive signs on the hiring front. In roughly the first five months of 2025, the agency received more than 22,000 job applications, the Department of Homeland Security said at the time. That marked a more than 200% increase over the same period in 2024, officials said.

Despite that success, the number of new hires dropped off slightly in 2025 following a spike in onboarding in President Joe Biden’s last year in office, according to OPM data.

Guglielmi said the agency is on track to exceed hiring goals in fiscal 2026, with more than 1,000 new special agents and more than 400 Secret Service Police officers expected to be hired by the end of September.

The contract was awarded to Avvy on an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity basis, meaning its final terms are flexible based on what the Secret Service demands and what the contractor can deliver. Federal regulation states a preference for awarding such contracts to multiple vendors, though in this case the Secret Service chose just one.

Avvy is a “joint venture” of two other firms — Arillic and the larger DCG, both based in Virginia. They have formed a partnership under the Small Business Administration’s Mentor-Protege program, which enables larger companies to win contracts set aside for small businesses in exchange for providing support to the smaller firm.

Arillic has won a few federal contracts, according to government records, with the largest being a $3.5 million award to the Health and Human Services Department. DCG has won hundreds of contracts collectively worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Some of DCG’s contracts have involved communications and advertising for the Department of Veterans Affairs and the U.S. Army’s public affairs office.

Arillic CEO Arthur Tamayo said a combination of both teams would provide the work. In a brief phone call, he said he appreciated NOTUS’ interest in the contract, noting there was “a lot of crazy stuff coming out” in the government contracting space lately including “people turning the Reflecting Pool green.” Tamayo, who is also listed as the point of contact for Avvy, did not answer detailed questions about the Secret Service contract. DCG did not respond to a request for comment.

While Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection have set significantly larger hiring targets in Trump’s current term, the Secret Service contract appears to be the largest award the department has provided to one company for recruiting or hiring since he came back into office.

In Trump's first term, CBP signed a $300 million contract with Accenture to help it bring on 7,500 border personnel and solicited offers for a similar contract at ICE. DHS canceled the CBP contract after Accenture only successfully helped the agency hire 15 employees and aborted the ICE contract before it got off the ground.

Jeff Neal, a long-time career federal human resources official who most recently led DHS’s personnel shop, said it was not unusual for agencies to seek outside help when looking to surge hiring. But he said he didn’t think the applicant goals were realistic.

“The thing I question,” he added, “is a company that doesn’t have experience. But that appears to not be out of the ordinary for this administration.”
