entries.title: Inspection Finds ‘Systemic Breakdown’ in D.C Police’s Crime Reporting
entries.summary: A new report from the city’s inspector general found that the department’s policies around crime data are outdated or incomplete.
entries.content:
Crime reporting oversight at D.C.’s police department experienced a “prolonged, systemic breakdown” over the past decade as the department operated with outdated policies and failed to properly review its crime reports for accuracy, the city’s inspector general found in an investigation released Tuesday.

The inspector general’s report adds to a growing number of probes into crime statistics and reporting at the department, including an internal investigation that resulted in the proposed firing of 13 top police officials and investigations by the Department of Justice and Congress that heaped scrutiny on D.C. police leadership.

In addition to roiling the department for the past year, the inquiries have placed the city in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, which has been eager to flex its authority over the nation’s capital. Last year, when President Donald Trump took the unprecedented step of seizing temporary control of the city police department despite a precipitous drop in violence, he justified the move by alleging that police officials had manipulated crime statistics to make the city appear safer than it actually was.

Now, the inspector general’s report — and the response from interim D.C. Police Chief Jeffery Carroll, who said he agreed with all of its findings and was already taking steps to reform the department’s crime-reporting practices — chart one path forward for the department as it continues to wrestle with the fallout from the controversy.

Police officers and close observers of crime generally do not doubt that the city has grown significantly safer after a generational spike in violent crime in 2023. Homicides — perhaps the most challenging crime to conceal — have dropped every year since, according to D.C. police data.

The OIG audit did not examine whether the department has been reporting crime statistics accurately. Instead, investigators looked into whether the department had adequate quality-control systems for crime data and reporting. They found several significant shortcomings. 

A spokesperson for D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, who requested the inspector general's investigation, declined to comment on the findings.

NBC4 Washington was first to report on a draft of the report.

The police department shut down an independent unit that reviewed crime reports for accuracy in 2013, and its records system also failed to flag reports with classification errors or incomplete narratives, leaving them uncorrected, the report said.

In the absence of an independent review unit, ensuring the accuracy of crime reports fell on district commanders and their teams, who are stretched for time, and identifying mistakes “depended largely on individual initiative rather than structured oversight,” investigators wrote.

The police department’s policies are also outdated and incomplete, according to the report, which said that officers are subject to a “patchwork of overlapping and sometimes conflicting policies” on how to report crime. About a third of the department’s general orders, the rules that govern officer behavior, are more than 20 years old. Some of the policies about crime reporting reference the independent review unit that no longer exists, for example, or refer to a computer system that the department no longer uses. And, significantly, no single document describes how crime should be classified and reported from start to finish, according to the audit.

Investigators also found that cultural issues have hampered the department: In interviews, officers described an environment where they felt hesitant to express concerns about crime reporting because they feared retaliation and had no way to submit anonymous complaints.

The report noted that concerns about crime statistics are not unique to the District.

“Research has consistently found that when the same personnel responsible for crime reporting are also the ones whose performance is measured by that crime data, there is an inherent incentive to influence the numbers,” it said. 

The department has already taken some steps over the past several months to address the concerns brought up by the audit, the report said, including launching mandatory training on crime classification for officers and starting to reestablish an independent unit to review police reports for quality and accuracy. Carroll, in a letter responding to the audit, said he agreed with all of its core findings and said his goal was to ensure “strict accountability across the department.”

As Carroll seeks to tackle the systemic problems identified by the inspector general, lengthy discipline proceedings will continue for the top officials accused of improperly changing or manipulating crime reports. Those discipline recommendations came out of a 554-page internal affairs investigation that painted a picture of a department where officials struggled with immense pressure to reduce crime in their districts — pressure that led some of them to violate department policy, investigators allege.

Several police officials stand accused of pressuring officers to classify violent assaults, robberies and thefts as lesser offenses, according to a copy of the investigation, which concluded in the spring and has been reviewed by NOTUS. Others are accused of improperly editing police reports, either at the direction of a higher-up or of their own accord. The department has not released the investigation, in keeping with its policy of not revealing those disciplinary records to the public.

The internal probe, along with previous investigations conducted by the Justice Department and Republicans in Congress, also criticized the leadership of former D.C. Police Chief Pamela Smith, who resigned in December. Though she said she did not resign because of the inquiries into crime statistics, Smith’s departure came after a draft report from the Justice Department and a published report from Republicans on the House Oversight Committee both excoriated her leadership, accusing her of creating a climate of fear that incentivized commanders to artificially suppress reports of serious crimes.

The D.C. police internal affairs investigation featured interviews with officials who said Smith would frequently berate top command staff. It concluded that her treatment of those under her command had a “drastic and negative effect” on the department, but did not find that Smith had personally ordered anyone to misclassify a crime.

Smith has repeatedly denied claims that she manipulated statistics. Bowser defended the police chief, too; she requested the inspector general’s probe after the release of the DOJ and House Oversight probes, saying she hoped the city office would provide a less biased perspective.
entries.author: Jenny Gathright

entries.title: The FDA Is Officially Codifying DOGE-Era Changes
entries.summary: The agency will stop specializing its field inspectors starting in October.
entries.content:
The Food and Drug Administration will officially consolidate administrative staff across the agency’s nine centers and stop specializing its field inspectors starting in October.

The Trump administration approved the agency’s reorganization proposal, according to an internal agency announcement reviewed by NOTUS. In the announcement, Melanie Keller, the FDA’s deputy commissioner for operations and chief operating officer, said the reorganization proposal known as “Simple Reform” will go into effect on Oct. 1.

Under the revised structure, individual centers like the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research will no longer conduct their own administrative affairs like human resources, finance and information technology services. Instead, the agency will operate under a “shared service” model in which the FDA Office of Operations controls those functions across the agency.

The agency will also stop assigning its specialized field inspectors, who oversee the safety of medical products and clinical trials, to specific subject areas. Instead, they’ll operate as generalists and conduct inspections and investigations across multiple industries.

“Shared Services seeks to maximize efficiency and consistency,” the internal FDA website detailing the plan states.

Some former agency staff criticized the changes as not understanding how specialized different aspects of the agency are. One former acting commissioner, Janet Woodcock, called the changes a “mindless approach” and a “really, really bad idea” when the proposal was first announced in 2025, according to the regulatory news publication Pink Sheet.

The reorganization will not drastically change the roles and responsibilities of the agency’s nine centers. Nor will it result in any current FDA employees losing their jobs, according to the internal agency web page.

The changes formalize shifts to the agency’s operations and administrative structure that were put in place by the Trump administration over the past 18 months. Like other agencies across the Health Department, many of the FDA’s administrative staff were let go in the reductions-in-force led by DOGE in 2025. The agency let go a total of 3,500 employees in the DOGE cuts and is now hiring about 2,200 new employees.

The FDA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reorganization.

Steven Grossman, a regulatory consultant who writes the blog FDA Matters, said that while he wasn’t familiar with the specific changes proposed, he was concerned that they could oversimplify an agency that’s complicated for a reason.

“Centralization is not always good and efficient,” Grossman said, adding that it “often leaves functions understaffed. It often misses the contours of how work is actually done.”

Some experts also pointed out that the changes will generalize the duties of inspectors who oversee medical products and clinical research. The agency moved in 2017 to place inspectors within specific programs of expertise, rather than requiring them to work across multiple programs. The approved plan would reverse that change.

“Proper assessment requires FDA investigators with matching skills and knowledge, and it’s absurd to expect ‘generalists’ to develop those traits,” Steven Silverman, a former director of the FDA Office of Compliance, Center for Devices and Radiological Health, wrote in a blog post when the proposal was announced. “How and why would a generalist build these strengths while going from a drug inspection one week to a biologics site the next with a device inspection the week after?”
entries.author: Margaret Manto

entries.title: Beshear Pushes McConnell to Resign or ‘Provide Proof’ He’s Fit to Serve
entries.summary: Sen. McConnell has not been seen in public since mid-June.
entries.content:
Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, gave Sen. Mitch McConnell an ultimatum on Monday: Provide more information about his ongoing health struggles and his ability to return to the Senate, or resign from office.

“As Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign,” Beshear wrote in a letter to the longtime senator’s office obtained by NOTUS.

The letter, first reported by CNN, came on the heels of a statement released by McConnell Monday, announcing that he is still not cleared to return to the Senate and is focusing on “intense physical therapy.” The update included another picture of the senator and his wife, Elaine Chao, but did not include many details about his condition or an expected return date.

McConnell added that he would be unable to attend Kentucky’s Fancy Farm event this Saturday, which is the state’s long-standing bipartisan political rally.

“There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” McConnell said in the statement.

The Office of the Attending Physician stated that McConnell is continuing to recover, but Beshear took issue with the lack of details about the senator’s physical condition.

“Even the attending physician’s written statement does not discuss your actual condition, including whether you can speak, reason, or carry out your duties as a senator,” Beshear wrote.

The governor addressed the letter to McConnell but called on his Senate staff to be “honest and transparent” with Kentuckians if the senator is unable to reply.

“I am addressing this letter to Senator McConnell under the assumption that he is capable of reading and responding verbally, and not incapacitated by means of consciousness or cognition,” Beshear wrote. “If the Senator is unable to respond for either of those or other conditions, consider this letter a demand for his Senate staff to be honest and transparent with the people of Kentucky.”

McConnell’s office did not comment on the governor’s letter.

Beshear sent the letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune along with an additional letter calling on him to investigate McConnell’s absence.

“I think that's an issue, really, that’s between Sen. McConnell and the people of Kentucky,” Thune said when asked about the letter. “I’m not sure what [Beshear’s] prerogatives are in that case, but that’s where the issue should be resolved.”

If McConnell steps down, a special election is required to fill his vacant Senate seat, according to a 2024 state law. A 2021 law would have allowed Beshear to choose a replacement for McConnell from a list of three Republicans provided by the outgoing senator.

But the governor signaled that he might be willing to challenge the law.

“There is a Kentucky constitutional provision that says that I appoint all state officers when there’s a vacancy,” Beshear told MS NOW earlier this month. “The question is, does that apply to federal offices? Well, before there was ever a law in Kentucky on how this would work, multiple appointments were made by governors, presumably under that provision.”

McConnell has not been seen in public since his hospitalization on June 14. The senator’s office has released statements saying he is receiving medical treatment after suffering a fall and was "briefly unconscious” after the initial incident.

As a survivor of childhood polio, McConnell has said that the illness still impacts his mobility. The senator had been seen using a wheelchair at the Capitol following a previous fall.

This article has been updated with a comment from Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Judge Allows Trump to Refile His $15 Billion New York Times Defamation Suit
entries.summary: An amended complaint must be filed by Aug. 27.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Florida is allowing President Donald Trump to amend and refile his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times after the publication moved to toss the case on First Amendment grounds.

The amended complaint must be filed by Aug. 27, United States District Judge Steven D. Merryday ruled Monday. Merryday, who was appointed by former President George H. W. Bush, postponed a ruling on the Times’ motion to dismiss the case.

Trump’s legal team sued the Times in September 2025, claiming that three articles and a book written by Times’ journalists contained “repugnant distortions and fabrications about President Trump.” The complaint argued that the book and articles, which were published ahead of the 2024 election, sought to maliciously harm Trump’s “worldwide reputation for success.”

Trump and Trump-backed organizations have continually sued — and lost — defamation cases against news publications. In April, a federal judge tossed Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal after it reported that a sexually suggestive letter with the president’s signature had been gifted to disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

And in July, a separate federal judge in Florida dismissed a $3.8 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, against The Washington Post over an article about a mysterious financial entity’s connection to the Trump-owned social media platform.

The Times, which has been repeatedly sued by Trump, argued that Merryday should either dismiss the case or have it transferred to the Southern District of New York. After Merryday denied the newspaper’s motion to move the case, Trump celebrated on Truth Social.

Lawyers for both parties delivered oral arguments for more than two hours on July 22. Merryday’s ruling on Monday did not indicate what parts of Trump’s original complaint could be amended.

Trump’s legal team had proactively requested for Merryday to grant them an amended complaint that would “cure any … deficiencies” and show evidence of how “the Challenged Statements are not substantially true, along with additional facts and innuendo by Defendants to show why the Challenged Statements are defamatory, and additional evidence of actual malice for each Defendant.”

The Times will have 21 days to file a response after the amended complaint is submitted, Merryday said.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
